target: जो बस पहले आएगी, हम वही ले लेंगे।
english: We'll take whichever bus comes first.
reason: Preachy proverb / textbook motto ("the one who works hard is the one who succeeds"). Replacement keeps the same जो … वही relative pattern in an ordinary everyday decision.

target: वह मेरा दोस्त है जो बगल वाले घर में रहता है।
english: He's my friend who lives in the house next door.
reason: Moralising proverb about true friendship, not something anyone says in conversation. Replacement keeps the वह … जो relative-clause pattern with everyday content.

target: जो आम आपने भेजे थे, वे बहुत मीठे थे।
english: The mangoes you sent were very sweet.
reason: Dictionary-definition trivia about custard apple, and it doesn't even contain the node's जो/वह relative structure. Replacement teaches the relative clause with common fruit vocabulary.

target: सोना चाँदी से महँगा होता है।
english: Gold is more expensive than silver.
reason: Encyclopedic trivia ("gold is a rarer metal") in written register; दुर्लभ is well above this level. Same से comparative, same nouns, but a comparison someone would actually make.

target: यह कमरा उस कमरे से बड़ा है।
english: This room is bigger than that room.
reason: Geology trivia — a learner will never compare granite with marble. Replacement keeps the से comparative in an everyday situation.

target: प्लास्टिक की कुर्सी लकड़ी की कुर्सी से हल्की होती है।
english: A plastic chair is lighter than a wooden chair.
reason: Materials-science trivia (bamboo vs wood flexibility), same textbook mould as the other node-15 cards. Replacement keeps से ज़्यादा-style comparison and the लकड़ी vocabulary with a usable comparison.

target: मिक्सी से चटनी बनाने में दो मिनट लगते हैं।
english: It takes two minutes to make chutney in the mixer.
reason: Energy-policy factoid in written/officialese register, not everyday speech. Replacement keeps the identical "X से … बनाने में …" instrumental pattern in a kitchen context.

target: चौदह अप्रैल को मेरी बहन की शादी है।
english: My sister's wedding is on the fourteenth of April.
reason: Calendar/civics trivia in official register; a learner practising dates needs to talk about their own plans. Same date + को pattern.

target: दुकानदार ने सामान थैले में रख दिया।
english: The shopkeeper put the things in the bag.
reason: घुमक्कड़ is a literary word almost nobody uses, and "the wanderer travelled the whole world" is storybook filler. Replacement keeps an agent noun + ने-perfective in a real situation.

target: बल्लेबाज़ ने छक्का मारा तो सब ताली बजाने लगे।
english: The batsman hit a six and everyone started clapping.
reason: "मैदान गुँजा दिया" is flowery commentary register no learner will produce. Replacement keeps बल्लेबाज़ + छक्का मारना in plain spoken Hindi.

english: Deepak got tired and fell asleep.
reason: Word-for-word duplicate of hi-2026 with only the name changed — pure padding. Replacement keeps the conjunctive participle + compound verb pattern with different content.

target: थककर उसने तकिये पर सिर रख दिया।
english: Tired, she put her head down on the pillow.
reason: Subjectless novel-style fragment padded with decorative adjectives (नरम गुदगुदे), and सिर रखा isn't the compound verb the node teaches. Replacement supplies a subject and the रख दिया compound.

target: जल्दी निकलने से हम समय पर पहुँच गए।
english: Because we left early, we reached on time.
reason: Essay/report register ("getting the scholarship made further studies easier") rather than spoken Hindi. Replacement keeps the same "-ने से" cause pattern in an ordinary sentence.

target: पैर में चोट लगने पर डॉक्टर ने प्लास्टर चढ़ा दिया।
english: When he hurt his leg, the doctor put a cast on it.
reason: Agentless medical-report register ("a plaster was applied") where everyday speech is being taught. Replacement keeps the "-ने पर" pattern with a subject and normal spoken phrasing.

target: मेले में हाथ से बनी चीज़ें बिकती थीं।
english: Handmade things used to be sold at the fair.
reason: Bureaucratic exhibition-report phrasing, and "हाथों के काम की चीज़ें" is awkward Hindi (natural is हाथ से बनी चीज़ें). Replacement keeps the past-habitual pattern in ordinary speech.
